record.paper_title: Open Problems in Geometric Methods for Instance-Based Learning
record.original_question: Let {X, Y} be a training set of n labeled patterns in d dimensions, and let C be the condensed training-set-consistent subset produced by Hart's condensed nearest neighbor rule. A naive brute-force algorithm computes C in O(dn^3) time. By how much can the complexity of computing this condensed subset be reduced?

evidence.quote: using a naive brute-force algorithm the complexity of computing the condensed subset of {X, Y } is O(dn3). In practice no efforts have been made to use other than brute-force algorithms. It is an open problem to determine how much this complexity can be reduced.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\{X, Y\} = \{(x_i, y_i) : 1 \le i \le n\}$ be a training set of $n$ labeled patterns, where each $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and each $y_i$ is a class label drawn from a finite set. For a subset $S \subseteq \{X, Y\}$, define the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier $\mathrm{NN}_S$ which assigns to a query point $q \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the label of the closest point in $S$ under the Euclidean metric (ties broken by some fixed rule). A subset $C \subseteq \{X, Y\}$ is said to be training-set-consistent if $\mathrm{NN}_C(x_i) = y_i$ for every $i = 1, \ldots, n$.

Hart's Condensed Nearest Neighbor (CNN) rule produces such a consistent subset $C$ by the following procedure: initialize $C$ with one arbitrary labeled pattern; then repeatedly scan the remaining points of $\{X, Y\}$, and for each point $(x_i, y_i)$ for which $\mathrm{NN}_C(x_i) \neq y_i$, add $(x_i, y_i)$ to $C$. Repeat the scanning process until an entire pass through the training set produces no additions to $C$. The output $C$ depends on the order of scanning, but in all cases the naive brute-force implementation of this rule runs in time $O(d n^3)$.

Determine the best possible worst-case time complexity, as a function of $n$ and $d$, for computing a subset $C$ produced by Hart's CNN rule. In particular, by how much can the $O(d n^3)$ bound of the brute-force algorithm be improved?
artifact.status_search_result: The Fast Condensed Nearest Neighbor (FCNN) rule by Angiulli (ICML 2005) achieves a subquadratic worst-case time complexity for computing a training-set-consistent subset, improving substantially on the cubic brute-force bound. However, FCNN does not reproduce Hart's specific output, and the precise optimal complexity of computing a Hart CNN-condensed subset is not known to be fully settled.

status_evidence.title: Fast Condensed Nearest Neighbor Rule (Angiulli, ICML 2005)
status_evidence.snippet: The FCNN rule is order independent and has subquadratic worst case time complexity, while it requires few iterations to converge.
status_evidence.claim: A subquadratic-time algorithm exists for computing a training-set-consistent subset, improving on the cubic brute-force complexity, though it is a variant rather than Hart's exact rule.

status_evidence.title: The condensed nearest neighbor rule (Hart, 1968)
status_evidence.snippet: Hart's original CNN rule with no specified efficient implementation.
status_evidence.claim: Original CNN rule whose brute-force implementation runs in O(dn^3).
